questions.stem: A factory can produce 12,000 units a month and currently produces 9,000. What is capacity utilisation?
questions.why: Capacity utilisation = (current output / maximum output) x 100 = (9,000 / 12,000) x 100 = 75%.
whyNot: This divides maximum by current, the wrong way round.
That is spare capacity in units, not a percentage.
This is a decimal point error.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of capacity?
options: The maximum output a business can produce in a period with its existing resources
The output a business currently produces
The amount a business can sell
The number of employees a business has
questions.why: Capacity is the ceiling set by the resources the business has. Utilisation measures how much of that ceiling is being used.
whyNot: That is current output.
That is demand, which may be above or below capacity.
Headcount is one input to capacity, not capacity itself.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $36,000 a month. What happens to fixed cost per unit when output rises from 9,000 to 11,000 units?
questions.why: 36,000 / 9,000 = $4.00. 36,000 / 11,000 = $3.27. Raising utilisation cuts fixed cost per unit with no new investment at all, because the machinery and rent were already being paid for.
whyNot: This reverses the two figures.
The same fixed cost over more units gives a lower cost per unit.

questions.stem: Why is operating at 100% capacity utilisation usually undesirable?
options: There is no slack for breakdowns, maintenance, absence or an unexpected order
It is illegal to operate at full capacity
Fixed costs rise at full capacity
questions.why: Machines running flat out get no servicing and then fail, a profitable large order has to be turned down, and staff have no time for training or cover. Around 90% is the usual target.
whyNot: Unit costs are at their lowest near full capacity; the problem is risk, not cost.
There is no such restriction.
Total fixed costs do not change with output.

questions.stem: A business is under-utilised. Which response uses the spare capacity rather than reducing it?
questions.why: Subcontracting or producing own-label for a retailer fills the idle capacity and earns a contribution from assets that are already being paid for.
whyNot: That is rationalisation, which reduces capacity.
Also rationalisation.
Also rationalisation.

questions.stem: What is the key judgement when deciding whether to rationalise after a fall in demand?
options: Whether the fall in demand is temporary or permanent
Whether the business is a limited company
Whether the business uses flow production
questions.why: Temporary means keep the capacity and bridge the gap; permanent means cut it. Rationalising a seasonal dip means paying redundancy for capacity you will need again in three months, and it is hard to reverse.
whyNot: Legal form does not determine the answer.
Relevant to how it is implemented, not to whether it is right.
The production method does not determine whether demand will return.

questions.stem: A guesthouse sells 210 room nights in a 30-day month with 10 rooms. What is its capacity utilisation?
questions.why: Maximum capacity = 10 rooms x 30 days = 300 room nights. Utilisation = (210 / 300) x 100 = 70%.
whyNot: This divides by 1,000 or misreads the capacity figure.
That is the number of days, not a utilisation figure.
A decimal point error; utilisation cannot exceed 100%.

questions.stem: Which response to over-utilisation improves the margin as well as easing the pressure?
questions.why: Raising the price reduces the quantity demanded to a manageable level and earns more on each unit sold, so it eases capacity pressure and widens the margin at the same time.
whyNot: It adds capacity and adds cost.
It adds output and the subcontractor takes a margin.
It adds capacity at significant capital cost.

questions.stem: Why can a seasonal business not be judged on its annual capacity utilisation?
options: It may be near 100% in the peak and around 30% in the trough, and the average hides both problems
Seasonal businesses have no fixed capacity
questions.why: Both problems occur in the same year and need opposite responses: discount and market the low season to lift utilisation, and raise rates in the peak to manage demand. An average of 65% would suggest neither.
whyNot: They can be, and the average is the problem.
It applies to hotels, restaurants, airlines and any capacity-constrained service.
Room numbers are precisely a fixed capacity.
